cornish-game-hen-roasted-skin-not-eaten.title: Cornish Game Hen (roasted, skin not eaten)

content.title: About
content.content: The Cornish game hen is a small domestic bird (about 500‑700 g) often served whole as a roasted dish. The skin is usually removed to reduce fat content. The meat is tender, light‑pink, and has a mild flavor that is similar to chicken but more aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the English county of Cornwall, where the bird was first bred in the 19th century.
Cornish game hens are considered a delicacy and are frequently served at festive meals.
Compared with regular chicken, they have a higher protein content and lower fat, especially when the skin is omitted.
The birds reach market weight in just 4‑5 weeks, making them a fast source of meat.
Traditionally they are seasoned with herbs, lemon, and garlic, and often served with wine‑based sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of roasted, skin‑less Cornish hen provides about 25 g of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin reduces saturated fat, making the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary patterns.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which support energy metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immune function, and bone health.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Because it contains virtually no carbohydrates, the hen does not raise blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: If the hen is brined or marinated in salty solutions, sodium intake should be monitored, especially for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hen whole, carving it into portions. It pairs well with roasted vegetables, potatoes, couscous, or salads. The skin can be saved for making a flavorful broth, but in this preparation it is not eaten.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh meat should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen, it can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

double-cheeseburger-on-white-bun-2-small.title: Double cheeseburger on white bun, 2 small patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double cheeseburger consists of two small beef patties, melted cheese, fresh vegetables and sauce, placed between a split white bun. It is a classic fast‑food item popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheeseburger appeared in the United States in the 1920s, and the double version became popular in the 1950s.
A white bun is usually made from wheat flour, butter and a touch of sugar, giving it a soft, slightly sweet texture.
Combining two patties with cheese increases the protein and calcium content compared with a single cheeseburger.
Some restaurants use hormone‑free beef to improve product quality.
Double cheeseburgers are often served with fries and a soft drink as a complete meal.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef patties provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese adds calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese supply B12, B6 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Vegetable nutrients
items.content: Lettuce, tomato and onion add fiber, vitamins and antioxidants.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A double cheeseburger can contain 600–800 kcal, making it unsuitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Saturated fat and sodium
items.content: Cheese and sauces increase saturated fat and salt levels, which may affect cardiovascular health if consumed frequently.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked patties may harbor bacteria such as E. coli, so they should be cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burger is typically eaten by hand, holding the bun. Add ketchup, mustard, mayo or barbecue sauce to taste. For a neater option, split the burger and eat with a fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burger in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze it and reheat in an oven or microwave before serving.

egg-substitute-omelet-scrambled-or-fried.title: Egg substitute, omelet, scrambled, or fried with cheese and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Egg substitute is a ready‑to‑use blend that allows you to make an omelet, scrambled eggs or fried dish without using real eggs. The formula typically contains plant proteins, starch, food‑grade additives and flavorings, plus spices. When mixed with water or plant milk, it can be sautéed with cheese and vegetables for a tasty, nutritious breakfast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg substitute is a staple in vegan cooking because it is completely plant‑based.
Many brands fortify the blend with vitamin B12 to mimic the nutrient profile of eggs.
Turmeric is often added to give the mixture a yellow hue similar to egg yolk.
The dry mix is shelf‑stable and does not require refrigeration until reconstituted.
Unlike real eggs, the substitute contains no cholesterol.

items.title: Low in cholesterol
items.content: The product contains no cholesterol, making it suitable for people monitoring blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Typical blends provide 10–15 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Formulations often include B12, riboflavin and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Starch and added fiber help promote regular bowel movements.

items.title: Allergy‑friendly for egg‑sensitive individuals
items.content: Absence of egg protein makes it safe for those with egg allergies.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Many substitutes are soy‑protein based, which can trigger reactions in soy‑allergic people.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions contain added salt, so individuals limiting sodium should check the label.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: Flavorings and preservatives may be present, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

items.title: Lower in certain minerals
items.content: Compared with real eggs, the substitute may be lower in iron and zinc.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Combine 1 part dry mix with 2–3 parts water (or plant milk), whisk until smooth and let stand 2–3 minutes. Heat a little oil in a pan, pour the batter, add shredded cheese and chopped vegetables (tomatoes, spinach, bell pepper). Cook until the edges turn golden, stirring if making scrambled style.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3–6 months. Do not keep the prepared liquid mixture; it should be made fresh before each use.

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans, cooked, are the young pods of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) that have been briefly boiled or steamed. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a tender‑crisp texture. Frequently used as a side dish, in salads, soups, and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are a good source of plant protein and dietary fiber.
Unlike dry beans, the whole pod is edible when young.
Short cooking retains most of the B‑vitamins and vitamin C.
They appear in many traditional cuisines: stir‑fried in Asian dishes, braised with olive oil in Mediterranean recipes.
Their flavonoid content provides antioxidant benefits for heart health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked green beans contain about 35 kcal per 100 g, making them ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B6, folate, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Vitamin C and antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, while flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains potassium, iron, and magnesium, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Undercooked beans can retain phytohemagglutinin, a toxin that may cause gastrointestinal upset.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked green beans can be served as a side, tossed into salads, added to soups, stews, pasta dishes, or baked in casseroles. They also freeze well for later use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked green beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: The hamburger slider is a miniature version of the classic burger, usually weighing 30–50 g, served in multiple pieces per portion. It consists of a small bun, a beef patty, cheese, pickles, onion and sauce. It is commonly offered in fast‑food outlets as a quick snack or as part of a combo.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sliders first appeared in the United States in the early 1980s as part of bar and fast‑food menus.
The name “slider” comes from the idea that the bite “slides” easily into the mouth, emphasizing speed and convenience.
In many countries sliders are served in sets of three or four, allowing diners to sample several flavors in one order.
Patty batches are often pre‑cooked and reheated on a grill or in a microwave to speed up service.
Sliders are a popular item in “speed‑eating” contests, where participants may consume up to 10 pieces in a minute.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburger sliders supply vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: The small size makes it easier to manage calorie intake compared with a full‑size burger.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Beef provides zinc, an important mineral for immune function.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: The patty and cheese can contain significant amounts of saturated fat, which may raise cardiovascular risk when consumed frequently.

items.title: Salt and sauces
items.content: Sauces and pickles often add a lot of sodium, potentially contributing to high blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bun is typically made from wheat flour, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Even though each piece is small, eating several sliders can quickly exceed daily calorie recommendations.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogens such as E. coli or salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sliders are usually eaten by hand, holding the bottom bun. They pair well with fries, barbecue sauce, or fresh vegetables. For a lighter option, add lettuce, tomato, or swap the beef patty for chicken or a plant‑based alternative.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared sliders in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen sliders keep well for up to 3 months; thaw completely and reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.
